name: Seated Guard Retention
description: An active defensive system while seated, using skeletal frames, foot posts, and leg mobility to block the opponent's pass and maintain guard layers.
shortInstruction: Keep feet on hips, maintain knee-elbow connection, use C-grips on wrists, and frame to recover or wrestle up.
summary: Active guard retention from seated position using frames, foot posts, and inside position.
whyItWorks: Keeps distance by using the longest levers (feet, shins) before the passer can close chest-to-chest.
Preserves inside position through knee-elbow connection and active hand fighting.
Turn frames into hip movement rather than pushing with arms.
Creates opportunities to wrestle up or re-attack when the passer overcommits.
commonMistakes: Letting feet dangle without a post on hips or biceps.
Opening space between knee and elbow, allowing underhooks.
Letting the opponent freely grip your pants or legs.
Pushing with straight arms instead of framing with forearms.
Fighting flat on the back instead of staying seated or on the side.
coachingCues: Feet on hips, elbows to knees.
Frame then move hips, not arms.

oneMinuteMode.goal: Maintain distance and inside position from seated guard.
steps: Keep both feet posted on hips or biceps.
Maintain knee-elbow connection on both sides.
Win the hand fight with C-grips on wrists.
React to the pass direction and pivot on your seat.
When they overcommit, wrestle up or re-guard.

safetySummary: Do not let your head get flattened toward the mat.
Protect your neck by keeping chin tucked during frames.
Avoid posting with straight arms to prevent joint locks.
keyCorrections: If they close the distance, your feet are not posting — bring them back to hips.
If they get an underhook, your knee-elbow gap is open — close it.
If they flatten you, you waited too long to frame or pivot.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Guard retention is a distance management game — your feet and frames are the first line of defense. React to the pass direction before committing to an escape or counter.

decisionTree.action: Keep both feet planted on their hips, pivot on your seat to face them, and maintain knee-elbow connection.

decisionTree.condition: Passer drops to both knees and tries to chest-to-chest
decisionTree.action: Extend your legs to create distance, frame on their biceps, and shrimp your hips back to reset.

decisionTree.condition: Passer grabs your pants or ankle
decisionTree.action: Strip the grip immediately with both hands (C-grip break) before they can control your leg.
Drop your elbow to the mat, turn to that side, and pummel your knee inside to regain inside position.
Use their momentum — frame off the biceps, elevate your hips, and wrestle up to a technical stand-up.

exitStrategies: If they pass one leg, recover half guard and restart the retention cycle.
If they flatten you completely, turn to your side, pummel the near knee, and re-establish seated guard.
If retention fails repeatedly, transition to supine guard with deep half as a backup layer.

moneyDetails: Always keep one foot on the hip to maintain distance; a dangling foot is a dead foot.
The C-grip on the wrist is your best friend — it kills their pant grip before it starts.
Pivot on your seat, not on your back; staying seated keeps your hips mobile.
nextStep: After retaining guard, look to wrestle up (technical stand-up), transition to supine guard, or attack with shin-to-shin entries.
fixItFast: They're past your feet? Frame with forearms and shrimp your hips out.
They have a pant grip? Strip it with both hands before they settle.
You're getting flattened? Turn to your side and pummel your knee inside.
